meta.title: Who really said "Follow your bliss and the universe will open doors for you where there were only walls"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Campbell's real line in The Power of Myth (1988) is 'doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be'. The 'walls' wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Follow your bliss and the universe will open doors for you where there were only walls'?
meta.ogDescription: His documented words, from The Power of Myth (1988), p. 120: 'doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be'. The 'walls' line is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Not his words — a paraphrase of Joseph Campbell
answer.authorDates: 1904–1987 · American mythologist and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College
answer.sourceLine: Campbell really did say the first three words — but not this sentence. His documented line, in The Power of Myth (Doubleday, 1988), p. 120, is “I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.” The version that invokes “the universe” and knocks down “walls” appears in no Campbell book, lecture or interview that anyone has been able to cite.

source.heading: What Campbell actually said

docMeta.dd: p. 120 — also spoken on camera in the PBS series, Ep. 4, ‘Sacrifice and Bliss’
Unsourced paraphrase — where a work is named at all, it is The Power of Myth, which does not contain this wording

source.excerpt: … if you do follow your bliss you put yourself on a kind of track that has been there all the while, waiting for you … I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section on Joseph Campbell ↗ gives the line as “I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be,” cited to The Power of Myth (book), p. 120.

Bill Moyers’ own site carries the transcript of Ep. 4, ‘Sacrifice and Bliss’ ↗, where Campbell speaks the same words — “doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be” — with no mention of walls or of the universe.

The Joseph Campbell Foundation’s own page on ‘Follow Your Bliss’ ↗ assembles his sourced statements on the idea, quoting the “didn’t know they were going to be” wording. The “walls” version is not among them.

A phrase search across the whole of English Wikiquote returns no occurrence of “where there were only walls” anywhere, while the Goodreads entry that spread it ↗ carries 964 likes and no book, lecture or date at all.
source.excerptNote: From Campbell’s reply when Bill Moyers asked whether he ever felt helped by hidden hands. Wikiquote cites the passage to The Power of Myth, p. 120; the same wording is transcribed in the broadcast series.

The popular “universe … walls” wording has no traceable source at all, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.kicker: The man who said the first three words
author.heading: Who Joseph Campbell was
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American mythologist and professor of literature
author.bio: Joseph Campbell was born in White Plains, New York on 26 March 1904 and died in Honolulu on 30 October 1987. He taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College and wrote The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), the comparative-mythology study that gave popular culture the “hero’s journey.” His widest fame came posthumously, through the 1988 PBS conversations with Bill Moyers and their companion book, The Power of Myth — the source of many of the Campbell lines in circulation today, and of this one.

misattribution.heading: What got changed
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication invented from nothing — it is a real Campbell thought that was smoothed, inflated and then re-attributed to him in its improved form. Two things happened to the second half of his sentence.

items.who: “the universe will open doors for you”
items.why: Campbell’s sentence has no cosmic agent doing the opening. In the broadcast transcript ↗ the doors simply “open” — a description of what happens to you, not a promise made by the universe.

What he said was “where you didn’t know they were going to be” — doors you failed to notice, not walls miraculously breached. Wikiquote’s sourced text ↗ preserves the original phrasing, and the word “walls” appears nowhere in it.

The wording travels with a bare “— Joseph Campbell” and nothing else. The Goodreads page ↗ names no book, no lecture and no year, and Goodreads itself notes that its quotes are community-added and unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: Campbell’s actual sentence, sourced on Wikiquote to The Power of Myth, p. 120 ↗: “I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.”

context.heading: Why the real line is better
lead: Campbell was not making a promise. Moyers had asked whether he ever felt helped by hidden hands, and Campbell answered with what he called a superstition that had grown on him: that following your bliss puts you on a track already there, waiting. The doors in his sentence were always doors — you simply hadn’t seen them. The paraphrase turns that into a transaction with the cosmos, which is close to the reading Campbell spent his last years resisting.

He was uneasy about how the slogan landed even in his own lifetime. Wikipedia’s biography ↗ records his rueful line that he should have told students to “follow your blisters” instead. The Joseph Campbell Foundation’s own gloss keeps the same edge, quoting him: “If your bliss is just your fun and your excitement, you’re on the wrong track.”
context.detailsSummary: Why almost every “Campbell quote” comes from one book
detailsBody: Campbell died in Honolulu on 30 October 1987. The Power of Myth — both the PBS series and the Doubleday companion book — appeared in 1988, the year after his death. That is part of why the conversations became his best-known work, and why so many of the “Campbell quotes” in circulation trace back to them rather than to his scholarly books such as The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949).

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section attributes "I say, follow your bliss and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be" to The Power of Myth (book), p. 120; the page contains no passage using the word "walls" in this connection, and its Disputed section lists only one unrelated quote.

Bill Moyers' official site hosts a full transcript of Ep. 4 'Sacrifice and Bliss' containing Campbell's words "follow your bliss, and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be."

The Joseph Campbell Foundation's 'Follow Your Bliss' page quotes "Follow your bliss and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be" (credited to Joseph Campbell and the Power of Myth with Bill Moyers) and "If your bliss is just your fun and your excitement, you're on the wrong track" (The Hero's Journey, 253); it nowhere uses the wording "the universe" or "walls."

Goodreads displays "Follow your bliss and the universe will open doors for you where there were only walls." attributed simply to Joseph Campbell, with 964 likes and no source work cited, and notes that quotes are community-added and not verified by Goodreads.
The Internet Archive's record for The Power of Myth gives Joseph Campbell (interviewee) and Bill Moyers (interviewer), publisher Doubleday, New York, publication year 1988, 231 pages.

Wikipedia gives Joseph Campbell's birth as 26 March 1904 in White Plains, New York and death as 30 October 1987 in Honolulu, Hawaii; describes him as an American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College; dates The Hero with a Thousand Faces to 1949 and the Power of Myth PBS series to 1988 with the book published by Doubleday; and records his remark that he should have said "Follow your blisters."
